title: Top 5 Weirdest Ways Animals Sleep 😴
hook: You think you sleep badly? Wait until you see how these 5 animals do it.
script:
You think you sleep badly? Wait until you see how these five animals do it.
Number five: sea otters.
They float on their backs and often hold paws, so they don't drift apart.
Some wrap themselves in kelp like a seatbelt.
Number four: sperm whales.
They nap hanging straight up and down, like giant floating pillars, for only ten to fifteen minutes.
Number three: the common swift.
This bird can stay airborne for about ten months straight.
Scientists think it even naps up there.
Number two: frigatebirds.
Researchers caught them sleeping mid-flight, in bursts of about twelve seconds.
That adds up to less than an hour of sleep a day.
Number one: wild African elephants.
A study found they sleep only about two hours a day, mostly standing up.
Sometimes they skipped a whole night.
So which one sleeps most like you?
Comment below.
And next time you think you sleep badly, wait until you see how these five animals do it.

title: 5 Funny Town Names With Wild Backstories
hook: These 5 real town names sound made up, but you could drive to every single one of them.
script:
These five real town names sound made up, but you could drive to every single one of them.
Number five: Accident, Maryland.
In the seventeen-fifties, two survey teams measured the exact same land by mistake.
So it got called Accident.
Number four: Hot Coffee, Mississippi.
A shop owner sold hot coffee to travelers on the road.
People loved it so much, the town got named after it.
Number three: Why, Arizona.
It sits where two highways form a Y.
But names had to be at least three letters, so Y became W-H-Y.
Number two: Truth or Consequences, New Mexico.
In nineteen-fifty, a radio show offered to broadcast from any town that renamed itself after it.
Hot Springs said, why not.
Number one: Boring, Oregon.
It's officially partnered with Dull, Scotland, and Bland, Australia.
Yes, really.

title: The Great Rubber Duck Escape of 1992 🦆
hook: A storm knocked 28,800 bath toys off a ship, and they ended up teaching you how the ocean moves.
script:
A storm knocked twenty-eight thousand eight hundred bath toys off a ship, and they ended up teaching you how the ocean moves.
It's January, nineteen ninety-two.
A cargo ship from Hong Kong hits a storm in the North Pacific.
Containers tumble into the sea.
One is full of plastic toys.
Yellow ducks, blue turtles, red beavers and green frogs.
The box breaks open, and they float away.
Ten months later, the first ones wash up in Alaska.
That's when ocean scientist Curtis Ebbesmeyer gets curious.
He asks beachcombers to report every toy.
Each sighting shows where the currents carried them.
Some got caught in a giant loop of current circling the North Pacific.
Some may have drifted north, into the Arctic ice.
A pile of bath toys became one of the most famous ocean drift experiments ever.
Found one on the beach? What would you name it? Tell me below.
Because a storm knocked twenty-eight thousand eight hundred bath toys off a ship…

title: 3 School Facts That Are Actually False
hook: 3 facts you probably still believe, and you have 3 seconds to guess which are false.
script:
Three facts you probably still believe, and you have three seconds to guess which are false.
Ready?
Fact one: goldfish only remember things for three seconds.
Three, two, one.
False!
Scientists have trained goldfish to respond to sounds and come back to them months later.
Your goldfish might actually remember you.
Fact two: you can see the Great Wall of China from space with your bare eyes.
Three, two, one.
False again!
NASA says it's very hard to spot from orbit, because it's narrow and the same color as the ground around it.
Fact three: bulls get angry when they see the color red.
Three, two, one.
Also false!
Bulls can't see red the way you do.
It's the cape's movement that gets their attention, not its color.
So how many did you get right? Zero, one, two, or all three?
Tell me in the comments, and be honest.

title: 3 Memory Tricks to Remember Anything
hook: If you've ever forgotten someone's name 5 seconds after hearing it, you need these 3 tricks.
script:
If you've ever forgotten someone's name five seconds after hearing it, you need these three tricks.
Trick one: test yourself instead of rereading.
In one famous study, students who quizzed themselves remembered more a week later than students who just reread.
So when you meet someone, say their name back, then try to recall it a minute later.
Trick two: chunk it.
Your brain can only juggle a handful of things at once.
That's why phone numbers come in little groups.
Long code? Shopping list? Break it into chunks of three or four.
Trick three: build a memory palace.
Picture a place you know really well, like your home.
Now place each thing you want to remember in a different room.
Memory champions use it, and in one study, regular people who practiced it got way better at remembering lists.
So which trick are you trying first?

title: Is That Really What I Sound Like?
hook: You've never actually heard your own voice. Not once. Here's why.
script:
You've never actually heard your own voice. Not once. Here's why.
Well, not the way everyone else hears it.
When you talk, your voice reaches your ears in two ways.
First, through the air, just like any other sound.
But second, through your own head.
The vibrations travel through the bones of your skull, straight to your inner ear.
And bone is great at carrying the low, deep parts of your voice.
So to you, your voice sounds richer and a bit deeper.
A recording only catches the air part.
No skull, no extra bass.
That's why it sounds higher and thinner, and kind of not like you.
Here's the funny part.
That recording is much closer to what your friends hear every single day.
So that voice you cringe at? Everyone already loves it.
Be honest, do you skip your own voice messages?
Tell me in the comments.
Because you've never actually heard your own voice…
